title: Institutional trust tracks perceived voice, socioeconomic security, partisan alignment, and the governance of public-sector AI
source_unit: OECD, OECD Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions 2026 Results: Navigating Rising Expectations and New Horizons
geography: OECD and participating partner countries in the 2025 Trust Survey and comparative institutional-trust analysis

observations.period: 2021-2025; partisan trust gaps in public institutions

denominator.unit: OECD countries with comparable trust information across the 2021, 2023, and 2025 survey waves

civil_service_gap.unit: percentage-point average partisan trust gap in the national civil service in 2025

gap_baseline.unit: percentage-point average partisan trust gap in 2021

non_supporter_trust.unit: percent trust among respondents who did not vote for the government in 2025, down from 47 percent in 2021

observations.method: OECD comparative analysis of repeated Trust Survey waves and political alignment, trust, and civil-service measures.
observations.uncertainty: Partisan trust gaps are descriptive associations and do not identify whether government performance, political messaging, identity, media, or policy disagreement caused the divergence.
observations.subgroup: Government supporters and non-supporters, people with different political agency, socioeconomic status, education, age, gender, and perceived discrimination.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some partisan differentiation can reflect legitimate disagreement or scrutiny rather than institutional failure; a common trust level is not automatically desirable.

denominator.unit: OECD participating-country comparison of national-government trust groups

discrimination_group_trust.unit: percent with high or moderately high trust among people identifying with a discriminated-against group

non_discrimination_group_trust.unit: percent with high or moderately high trust among people not identifying with such a group

trust_gap.unit: percentage-point trust gap associated with perceived discrimination

observations.method: OECD cross-country comparison of national-government trust by perceived discrimination and socioeconomic characteristics.
observations.uncertainty: Group differences are not causal estimates and may reflect overlapping income, education, political, institutional, and lived-experience factors.
observations.subgroup: People identifying with discriminated-against groups, people with financial concerns, lower- and higher-education groups, and marginalized populations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trust gaps can narrow when institutions improve access, representation, impartiality, and material security, but the report does not establish one universal remedy.

observations.period: 2025; interpersonal trust as an institutional-trust baseline

denominator.unit: OECD comparison of people with high versus low interpersonal trust

police_trust_high_interpersonal.unit: percent trusting police among people with high interpersonal trust

police_trust_low_interpersonal.unit: percent trusting police among people with low interpersonal trust

government_trust_high_interpersonal.unit: percent trusting national government among people with high interpersonal trust

government_trust_low_interpersonal.unit: percent trusting national government among people with low interpersonal trust

observations.method: OECD comparison of interpersonal trust and trust in public institutions across participating countries.
observations.uncertainty: Interpersonal and institutional trust are measured together in survey data; the gradient may reflect shared dispositions, social conditions, institutional experience, or reverse influence.
observations.subgroup: People with high or low interpersonal trust, users of public services, and groups with different experiences of government and police.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low interpersonal trust may be a rational response to social or institutional conditions rather than a stable individual trait.

observations.period: 2026; political agency, public-sector AI, and institutional legitimacy

denominator.unit: OECD trust-policy framework covering participation and public-sector AI

agency_trust_link.value: the share trusting national government is more than three times as high among people who feel people like them have a say in government decisions

ai_attitude.value: most people remain sceptical of AI deployed in the public sector, while views vary across population groups

policy_lever.value: responsiveness, participation, transparency, and governance choices are identified as levers for strengthening trust

observations.method: OECD synthesis of trust drivers, political-agency measures, day-to-day institutional interactions, and public-sector AI governance.
observations.uncertainty: The association between perceived voice and trust does not establish a causal effect; attitudes toward public-sector AI may change with use, performance, safeguards, and political context.
observations.subgroup: People with different perceived political voice, socioeconomic position, trust levels, and exposure to automated public services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Greater participation does not guarantee agreement, and public-sector AI can improve consistency or access when human oversight, explanation, and recourse are credible.

related_sources.claim: Canonical OECD publication record for the 2026 Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions.
Full OECD report covering trust over time, public-service interactions, complex policy decisions, public-sector AI, political voice, and legislative trust.

boundary: This record adds a publication-level socioeconomic-conditions-to-political-agency-to-institutional-trust route, including public-sector AI legitimacy. It is not a respondent-level survey analysis in this atlas, a causal trust model, an individual political-behavior panel, or a universal measure of institutional quality.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD 2026 report chapter and full-report navigation were reviewed; partisan trust gaps, socioeconomic and discrimination gaps, interpersonal trust gradients, political agency, and public-sector AI claims were cross-checked.
